title: Global Payments Report 2026: Transaction Banks Must Architect for an Agentic Future
gist: Transaction banks' straight-through-processing success masked a strategic threat: instant payments, agentic AI, and programmable money (stablecoins, tokenized deposits) are shifting corporate treasury toward machine-to-machine execution, and whoever controls the orchestration layer -- bank or fintech -- captures the higher-value client relationship.

themes.theme: Treasury automation hits an inflection point

insights.claim: Near-total straight-through-processing rates (nearly all domestic payments, over 90% of cross-border payments in many corridors) had lulled transaction banks into under-investing in agentic and generative AI, because the remaining manual share looked too small to matter.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Explains why incumbent banks are structurally behind on AI investment despite operational efficiency, a gap fintechs are now exploiting.
insights.locator: Transaction banking has spent decades automating

insights.claim: The convergence of instant payments, agentic AI, and programmable money (stablecoins and tokenized deposits executing via smart contracts) is pushing transaction banks' role beyond processing payments into participating in the decisions of when, where, and how money moves.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Reframes the competitive battleground for banks and payments fintechs from transaction execution to decision/orchestration rights -- a higher-margin layer.
insights.quote: the role of transaction banks will extend beyond processing payments to include participating in decisions that determine when, where, and how money moves.

themes.theme: Fintechs and TMS vendors are moving faster than banks

insights.claim: Ramp already grants AI agents direct access to corporate accounts to autonomously pay suppliers, issue cards, and transfer money, with humans limited to oversight, approvals, and anomaly review.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Signals agentic treasury execution is live in production today, not a future scenario -- a concrete competitive benchmark for incumbent banks' digital treasury offerings.
insights.locator: Others, such as Ramp, are going further

insights.claim: TMS providers Kyriba, Serrala, and Bottomline Technologies are embedding AI-native cash forecasting and risk tools directly into corporate ERP/treasury workflows, and Ripple Treasury manages fiat and digital assets simultaneously, disintermediating banks' traditional portal-based client touchpoint.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Watch these vendors as disintermediation risk for bank transaction-banking fee income; banks that don't embed comparable intelligence into client workflows risk losing the primary-adviser role.
insights.locator: Software providers and fintechs are already capitalizing

insights.claim: In a machine-to-machine treasury model, whichever provider controls the orchestration layer -- the logic that routes and governs agent-initiated transactions -- will own the client relationship and capture the higher-value work, not necessarily whoever executes the underlying payment.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Core investable thesis: value in payments is migrating from execution/settlement to orchestration control -- assess bank and fintech strategies by who is building that layer, not by payment volumes.
insights.quote: control of the orchestration layer will help determine the provider that ultimately owns the client relationship and captures the higher-value work.

themes.theme: Prior modernization gives incumbents an underrated advantage

insights.claim: The industry-wide migration to ISO 20022 messaging and the shift from batch to real-time processing already solved the main technical bottleneck to AI adoption by forcing standardized, rich data into every transaction layer, meaning incumbent banks have more AI-readiness than commonly assumed.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that banks are hopelessly behind fintechs on AI; the data infrastructure argument suggests incumbents can close the gap faster than expected if they act now.
insights.locator: Modernization during the past decade has given incumbent banks more muscle

themes.theme: Where banks should deploy AI first

insights.claim: Trade finance is stuck at a 30% to 70% straight-through-processing rate because of subjective document review, but AI document intelligence has already reached better-than-85% accuracy for early adopters, opening automation of the full trade life cycle from bills of lading to anti-money-laundering controls.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Trade finance is flagged as the highest-ROI near-term AI deployment area for banks given the wide STP gap and proven accuracy threshold already cleared.
insights.locator: Eliminate the document bottleneck in trade finance.

insights.claim: BNY has already proven AI-driven wire-repair automation at scale in live production, demonstrating that non-STP payment operations (the disproportionate cost driver among transactions) can be pushed toward zero-touch.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: A concrete production reference point for evaluating whether a bank's AI payment-operations claims are proven versus aspirational.
insights.locator: Move payment operations closer to zero-touch.

insights.claim: A BCG proof of concept using its agent-enabled Dark Software Factory with a global systemically important bank (G-SIB) delivered 20% to 40% efficiency gains in software engineering, positioning AI as a structural tool for legacy core-platform modernization rather than just a front-end feature.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Quantifies a real efficiency range for AI-assisted legacy modernization, useful for benchmarking bank tech-transformation budgets and timelines.

themes.theme: The client relationship is migrating from execution to governance

insights.claim: As AI agents assume responsibility for payment routing, liquidity, and risk decisions, the center of the corporate banking relationship shifts from executing transactions to owning the rules and intelligence that govern those decisions -- banks that embed this into client workflows can remain the primary adviser and orchestration partner.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Reframes the durable moat in transaction banking as governance/rules infrastructure, not payment volume or STP rate -- a lens for valuing bank transaction-banking franchises.
insights.quote: the center of the banking relationship will shift from transaction execution to the rules and intelligence that govern those decisions.

insights.claim: BCG prescribes a four-step sequence for banks to scale AI in transaction banking: quantify the cost of non-STP activity to rank use cases by value and difficulty; architect systems to expose secure, real-time data to AI agents with nonhuman-specific authorization and audit controls; close capability and control gaps in product, engineering, risk, and change management; and explicitly decide which parts of the agentic treasury layer to own versus source through a governed ecosystem of hyperscalers and AI providers.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/markus-ampenberger
insights.so_what: Gives investors a checklist for assessing whether a given bank's AI transaction-banking strategy is sequenced and credible versus purely experimental.
insights.locator: Rather than getting stuck in experimentation
